extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator / polite early-18th-century public (gentlemen and ladies interested in manners, arts, and morals)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted material comes from The Spectator (early-18th-century periodical essays and letters) offering judgments and advice about social behaviour, arts, love, and domestic amusements. The guidance is addressed to the polite reading public about how to act, judge, and find consolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgment for or against Kissing, by way of Civility or Salutation
rubrics_metrics.description: Country correspondents request 'your Judgment for or against Kissing, by way of Civility or Salutation' after a Town Gentleman adopts a fashion of publicly bowing and kissing women when entering rooms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the new fashion (courtier's repeated bows and taking the gross of the room, leading to young gentlewomen being kissed) is a proper civility or an indecent affectation; note rural inability to adopt such reserved airs and the potential impropriety and scandal it causes in country society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience decorum: no persons behind the scenes / making spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Behaviour of people who show themselves behind the scenes, leap over stage spikes, parade through doors, and otherwise make spectacle during a play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such activity 'diminish[es] the Pleasure of the Audience' and is presumptuous and unwarrantable; it has been made criminal by Her Majesty's command ('By her Majesty's Command no Person is to be admitted behind the Scenes'). Public self-display during performances is an intrusion on others' enjoyment and should be restrained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to relieve the Absence of Lovers
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical and invented methods for lovers separated by long absences to support themselves (e.g., set aside a punctual half-hour to think of one another; agreed prayers at an appointed hour; frequent letters; keeping portraits; revisiting shared places).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Scudery's lovers who each observed a stated half-hour to think of each other enjoyed mutual consolation; a couple used a prayer at a stated hour; the writer recommends applying oneself to family/estate duties but also recounts habits like reading the beloved's books, visiting his picture, frequent walks. Fantastical devices (the loadstone 'dial-plate') are presented playfully; the practical expedients are punctual shared time, prayer, correspondence, and keeping memorials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Features of a truly good/wise Picture (criteria for judging paintings)
rubrics_metrics.description: A good picture is 'begun on the Foundation of Geometry, carried on by the Rules of Perspective, Architecture, and Anatomy, and perfected by a good Harmony, a just and natural Colouring, and such Passions and Expressions of the Mind as are almost peculiar to Raphael.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish 'a picture made for the Eyes only' (merely gaudy colouring) from one that imitates nature and has studied composition; require technical foundations (geometry, perspective, anatomy), natural colouring, harmony, and appropriate expression; use reasoned observation of nature to form judgments rather than being dazzled by showy effects; one forcible light to catch the eye and emphasize the hero/object is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue is naturally amiable; which qualities make it lovely
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue is 'of an amiable Nature' and particularly those virtues which dispose us to do good to mankind — Justice, Charity, Munificence — are most beloved. 'The two great Ornaments of Virtue... are Chearfulness and Good-Nature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value qualities that render a person beneficial to others; temperance, faith, devotion are laudable but less publicly beloved than justice and charity; cheerfulness and good-nature keep virtue attractive and prevent severity and censoriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Esteem virtue even in political or personal opponents
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not let party hatreds or political differences blot out the merit of virtuous persons; 'Men of Virtue, though of different Interests, ought to consider themselves as more nearly united with one another, than with the vicious Part of Mankind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise and respect virtuous qualities in rivals or enemies; avoid blackening or defaming persons of undoubted probity because of political disagreement; condemn those who exploit religion or reputation to attack virtuous opponents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding ridicule and ingratitude (against the 'Apes')
rubrics_metrics.description: Condemnation of a group of women ('the Apes') who are 'both ugly and ill-natured' and who 'endeavour to detract from or ridicule every thing that appears so in others,' using nicknames and cruel mockery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ridicule, nicknames, and the mimicking of neighbours are 'in the highest Degree that Vice which is said to comprehend all others.' Advice: put deserving people on guard against such behaviour and aim to reform or expose it; value gratitude and civility over malicious mirth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation of female literature and learning relative to household peace
rubrics_metrics.description: A correspondent asks for 'the Difference between a Gentleman that should make Cheesecakes and raise Paste, and a Lady that reads Locke, and understands the Mathematicks' and requests guidance 'to make it consistent with the Quiet of such whose Fate it is to be liable to its Insults.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate moderation in female learning when it disturbs household peace; seek a balance that permits learning without imposing intellectual affectations that upset domestic tranquility; the aim is to regulate female literature to be compatible with the quiet of others in the household.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of modesty and civility in public travel and mixed company
rubrics_metrics.description: Complaint about a 'rude Fellow in a Stage-Coach' who uttered indecent language to women travellers, producing deep shame and distress among the modest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reiterate invectives against licentious behaviour in public places (coaches, play boxes, assemblies, pews); such behaviour inflicts severe suffering on modest persons and should be publicly admonished and discouraged—possibly by social sanctions or defensive action from offended parties' protectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommend innocent domestic pastimes over fashionable entertainments
rubrics_metrics.description: Request for guidance on 'innocent Diversions' for winter nights that are proper for families who do not attend operas or play-houses; cited games include Hot-Cockles, Questions and Commands, Mottoes, Similes, Cross-Purposes, Blind-Man's Buff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer games that are merry and innocent (avoid gambling games like Whisk, Lanterloo, or One and Thirty); value pastimes that include exercise and social humour without corrupting influences; examples show family entertainment (Blind-Man's Buff) producing wholesome mirth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Speculations to inform the innocent about the ways of men
rubrics_metrics.description: The Specator's papers aim to give 'the Virtuous and the Innocent... an Insight into the Ways of Men' so they can avoid snares of the crafty without being vitiated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide practical, worldly knowledge to the inexperienced to prevent exploitation; this is an admonition that moral goodness combined with ignorance of the world can make one vulnerable, so instruction should open minds while preserving virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive Stoic pedantry in praising virtue (virtue vs affectation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stoics are criticised for ascribing all good qualities (even physical beauty) to the virtuous man; this is 'more like a Philosophical Rant' than genuine wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise virtue for its amiable qualities but avoid hyperbolic or pedantic claims that virtue literally transforms every aspect of a person; maintain proportion and reason when celebrating moral excellence.
